passages.t: A tribe missing, and an oath
passages.happening:
At Mizpah the men of Israel had sworn an oath: “Not one of us will give his daughter in marriage to a Benjamite” (verse 1).

Now the people come to Bethel and sit before God until evening, weeping bitterly. “Why, O LORD God of Israel,” they cried out, “has this happened in Israel? Today in Israel one tribe is missing!” (verses 2-3). The next day they build an altar and offer sacrifices (verse 4).

They had also sworn a second oath, that anyone who did not come up to the assembly at Mizpah would be put to death (verse 5). They grieve for Benjamin. “Today a tribe is cut off from Israel. What should we do about wives for the survivors, since we have sworn by the LORD not to give them our daughters in marriage?” (verses 6-7).
passages.hearers:
The war is over, and Israel looks at what it has done. A whole tribe is almost gone. The twelve tribes were one people by covenant, and even in its disorder Israel knows it is not whole without Benjamin. Its grief is real.

But look at the question they put to God: ‘Why ... has this happened in Israel?’ They speak as though it had simply happened to them. They had sworn the oaths. They had burned the towns.

No answer from the LORD is recorded. The book began with Israel asking God's direction and receiving it. It ends with Israel asking why, hearing nothing, and making its own plans.

Oaths sworn before God were taken as binding, even when they were made rashly. That is why Israel does not simply cancel its vow not to give its daughters to Benjamin. The law allowed some vows to be set aside, but an oath sworn by the whole assembly was treated with great seriousness. Israel will keep both oaths, and the way it keeps them will cause more harm.
passages.later: The law held a vow as binding: “If a man makes a vow to the LORD or swears an oath to obligate himself by a pledge, he must not break his word” (Numbers 30:2). The wisdom books warn against words spoken rashly before God: “Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin” (Ecclesiastes 5:6).
passages.asks: Israel wept over a ruin it had made, and spoke as if it had simply happened. Ask whether you have ever grieved over something without admitting your own part in it. And ask what rash words, said in anger, you are still trying to keep, when they ought to be confessed instead.

passages.happening:
They ask which tribe did not come up to Mizpah, and they find that no one came from the town of Jabesh-gilead (verses 8-9).

So the assembly sends twelve thousand of its strongest men with an order: “Go and put to the sword those living in Jabesh-gilead, including women and children” (verse 10). They are to devote to destruction every man, and every woman who has been with a man (verse 11).

They find four hundred young women in Jabesh-gilead who have never been with a man, and they bring them to the camp at Shiloh (verse 12). The assembly sends a message of peace to the six hundred Benjamites at the rock of Rimmon. The Benjamites come back and are given the women from Jabesh-gilead, but there are not enough for all of them (verses 13-14).
passages.hearers:
Jabesh-gilead lay east of the Jordan, in Gilead. It had strong ties with Benjamin. Some readers think this story explains that bond, since many Benjamites would have been descended from the women of Jabesh-gilead.

The words ‘devote to destruction’ belong to the language of the conquest, a town given over wholly to God. Now Israel uses them against one of its own towns. And it spares the young women. That shows what the purpose really was. It was not devotion to God. It was finding wives.

This is told plainly, and it is terrible. A town is destroyed for staying away from an assembly. Its men, its married women and its children are killed. Four hundred young women see their families die and are handed to the men of the tribe that began the whole disaster. They are never asked, and they never speak.

The book does not present this as justice. It presents it as one more wrong committed to repair the damage of the last one.
passages.later: Jabesh-gilead's bond with Benjamin appears again. When the Ammonites besieged it, Saul, a Benjamite, came to its rescue (1 Samuel 11:1-11). And when Saul died, its men did not forget him: “all their men of valor set out, journeyed all night, and retrieved the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall of Beth-shan” (1 Samuel 31:12).
passages.asks: Israel tried to fix one wrong by doing another, and then another. Ask where you have tried to repair a harm you caused by causing a new one, and who paid for it. And think of the four hundred young women of Jabesh-gilead. Ask who, in the plans of the powerful around you, is being treated as a means to someone else's ends.

passages.t: The daughters of Shiloh, and the book's last words
passages.happening:
The people grieve for Benjamin, ‘because the LORD had made a void in the tribes of Israel’ (verse 15). The elders ask how they can find wives for the rest, since the women of Benjamin are dead and Israel has sworn not to give them its daughters (verses 16-18).

They remember the yearly feast to the LORD at Shiloh (verse 19). So they tell the Benjamites to hide in the vineyards and watch. When the young women of Shiloh come out to dance, each man is to seize one as a wife and take her home to Benjamin (verses 20-21). If the fathers or brothers complain, the elders will tell them to let it be, since they did not give their daughters and so have not broken the oath (verse 22).

The Benjamites do as they are told. They carry off as many of the dancers as they need, go home, rebuild their towns and settle there (verse 23). Then everyone goes home to his own tribe and land (verse 24).

“In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Shiloh was where the tent of God's house stood for much of the period of the judges. The careful directions to it in verse 19 have puzzled readers, since everyone would have known where Shiloh was. Some think they come from a time when the place had been destroyed and was less familiar. The yearly feast may be the same yearly pilgrimage later made by Samuel's parents, and the dancing in the vineyards suggests a harvest festival.

The plan is a form of marriage by capture known in the ancient world. Israel's law made no such arrangement for its own people. The elders' reasoning keeps the letter of their oath and ignores its spirit: the fathers did not give their daughters, so no one has broken his word. The daughters are simply taken.

They are taken at a feast to the LORD, while they dance. The narrator's flat way of telling it lets the reader feel how wrong it is.

Then comes the book's last verse, the refrain that framed these chapters. In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes. It is the book's verdict on everything it has told. The narrator presents these days as the depths of Israel's lawlessness, and never as a pattern.
passages.later:
A proverb puts the book's last sentence in its own words: “There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death” (Proverbs 14:12).

The yearly feast at Shiloh appears again at the start of the next story of Israel's leaders: “Year after year Elkanah would go up from his city to worship and sacrifice to the LORD of Hosts at Shiloh” (1 Samuel 1:3). The book of Ruth, set in these same days, ends with the name of David (Ruth 4:22).
passages.hard:
How can the Bible end a book with a mass killing and the seizing of women, with no word from God?

The ending is meant to unsettle. Judges does not present these events as models. It presents them as evidence of what Israel had become. The narrator's last verse is the book's verdict: this is what happens when there is no king and everyone does what is right in his own eyes. No word from the LORD is recorded after the people's question in verse 3. Israel seems to have stopped seeking him.

Readers differ on what the refrain looks toward. Many read it as a call for a king, perhaps David's line in particular. Others point out that the kings of Israel and Judah often led the people into the same idolatry, so the refrain cannot mean that any king would do. Some hear a longing for the LORD's own rule, which Gideon had named when he refused the crown. Others see a people so lost that only God's own act could restore them. Either way, the reader is meant to be troubled, and Scripture's refusal to soften these acts is part of its honesty about sin, including the sin of God's own people.

The women of Jabesh-gilead and the daughters of Shiloh are never asked and never speak. Like the woman of chapter 19, they are treated as a means to other men's ends. The flat report of their capture is part of the book's charge against Israel, not an approval of it. Any reading that makes these chapters a pattern for anything is a misreading.

A word for anyone who has been sold, traded, or forced to work or to do sexual acts by someone who controls them, or who is in that place now. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The book ends with a people doing what was right in their own eyes, and calling it a solution. Ask what it would look like for you, your family or your church to seek what is right in God's eyes instead. And ask what the young women of Shiloh would say to you if they could speak, and how you would answer them.
